comparison: Both evaluate the model architecture and methodology (C81-C83, C19, C49-C50). OpenEval finds the approach well-documented with appropriate physical assumptions and methods (SUPPORTED), while peer reviewers question novelty, cite missing prior work (Majmudar 2012), question the 100x drag coefficient adjustment, and note the 2D model applied to 3D behavior lacks justification (UNCERTAIN).

Both assess the model's reproduction of diverse behaviors including omega and delta turns (C45, C46, C71, C72, C84). OpenEval finds the capability demonstrated with methodological rigor (SUPPORTED), while peer reviewers note mixed views: turning behavior application is a strength but the 2D model applied to 3D turns lacks justification, and drag coefficients are likely incorrect when the worm touches itself (UNCERTAIN).

Both evaluate the novel mechanistic insight about deep bend propulsion (C47). OpenEval finds it supported by simulation data though experimental validation would strengthen it (SUPPORTED), while peer reviewers question whether the model produces new predictions, note results are primarily qualitative, and the 'newly discovered mechanism' claim lacks explicit validation (UNCERTAIN).

Both assess methodological details and computational tools (C63-C68). OpenEval finds the methods clearly documented with appropriate citations and transparency (SUPPORTED), and peer reviewers do not challenge these claims, noting computational efficiency and straightforward implementation as strengths (SUPPORTED). Full agreement on methodological documentation.

Both evaluate background claims about C. elegans biology and locomotion (C1-C5, C12-C16, C73-C77). OpenEval finds these well-established with appropriate citations (SUPPORTED), and peer reviewers implicitly accept them as established knowledge, noting 'grounding in empirical data' as a strength (SUPPORTED). Full agreement on background literature.

Both evaluate crawling validation (C24, C55, C26) with OpenEval also covering C56-C57. OpenEval finds simulated velocity matches experimental studies with visual support (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers affirm the model reproduces experimental data with realistic parameters, though note adjusted drag coefficients raise questions about parameter validity (SUPPORTED with reservations). Substantial agreement with caveats about parameters.

OpenEval evaluates swimming dynamics (C25, C27, C28) finding them consistent with physics but lacking direct experimental velocity comparison (SUPPORTED). Peer result R2 covers these claims alongside crawling (C24-C28), affirming reproduction of experimental movement data but questioning adjusted drag coefficients. Both support the results with parameter concerns.

OpenEval evaluates power analysis for escaping behavior (C29-C32, C40) finding quantitative analysis supported by simulation data but lacking experimental validation (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers identify increased power during omega turns as novel but note results are primarily qualitative without new predictions, and forces likely incorrect when worm touches itself (UNCERTAIN). OpenEval more positive than peer reviewers.

OpenEval evaluates power analysis for delta-turns (C34-C38, C40) finding patterns consistent with behavior but lacking experimental validation (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers group this with escaping behavior analysis, noting potential interest but emphasizing need for validation and questioning accuracy when worm self-contacts (UNCERTAIN). Similar divergence as R9/R4 pairing.

OpenEval evaluates claims about improvements over prior work (C58) finding the methodological advancement accurately contrasted with prior models (SUPPORTED). Peer result R6 covers C58-C60, directly challenging claims of improvement, stating the strength relative to prior approaches is not well supported and the claim is incomplete (UNSUPPORTED). Strong disagreement on novelty and improvement claims.

Both evaluate potential applications (C61-C62). OpenEval finds them promising but speculative without demonstration, making them uncertain as established results (UNCERTAIN). Peer reviewers affirm the model is straightforward and adaptable, treating these applications as reasonable extensions (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers more positive about potential applications than OpenEval.

Both evaluate novelty claims (C78-C80). OpenEval finds C78-C79 accurate but C80's novelty claim difficult to verify, making the claimed gap uncertain (UNCERTAIN). Peer reviewers explicitly challenge novelty, citing missing discussion of functionally similar 2012 work (Majmudar) and other uncited modeling approaches, indicating incomplete literature review (UNSUPPORTED for C80). Peer reviewers more critical of novelty claims.

OpenEval evaluates C78-C80 together finding prior work accurately cited but novelty uncertain. Peer result R12 evaluates only C78-C79, not disputing these background claims about prior modeling work though critiquing how the authors' work relates to them (SUPPORTED for C78-C79). Agreement on background claims but peer review addresses novelty separately in R7.

OpenEval evaluates crawling validation including force pattern consistency (C56-C57) as part of broader validation (SUPPORTED). Peer result R11 covers these comparative observations, not challenging them and emphasizing 'grounding in empirical data' as a strength (SUPPORTED). Agreement on these specific comparative claims.

OpenEval evaluates potential applications and model capabilities (C59-C62) finding C59-C60 supported by design but C61-C62 speculative (UNCERTAIN). Peer result R6 covers C58-C60 together, challenging improvement claims and stating the claim is incomplete (UNSUPPORTED for C58-C60 as a group). Disagreement stems from peer reviewers questioning the foundation for claimed advantages.

OpenEval evaluates established locomotion principles (C6, C7, C77) finding them well-supported by citations (SUPPORTED). Peer result R9 covers broader background including these claims, implicitly accepting them as established knowledge (SUPPORTED). Agreement on these background claims about locomotion mechanics.
